title: Characterization of the immune response after surgical intervention – a pilot study
summary:
Surgical procedures are associated with tissue trauma, which triggers a local and systemic inflammatory response in the body. This response involves activation of the immune system. Guided by these inflammatory signals, immune cells are recruited in large numbers to the site of tissue injury.

At the same time, compensatory mechanisms are initiated, which are a necessary prerequisite for wound healing. Pro- and anti-inflammatory processes are closely coordinated and induce an inflammatory reaction aimed at removing dead cells, reducing tissue damage, eliminating potential pathogens, and initiating the healing process. If this balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory mechanisms is disrupted, a dysregulated immune response may develop as a result of the surgical trauma. This dysregulation is associated with a wide range of postoperative complications, particularly impaired wound healing and infections.

Recently published studies suggest that the systemic inflammatory response is also associated with commonly observed postoperative organ dysfunctions, such as delirium or acute kidney injury. Unfortunately, the immune response to surgical intervention is still poorly understood.

This study aims to perform an in-depth characterization of immune cells in the context of surgical intervention and to correlate these findings with clinical course parameters related to organ dysfunction and recovery. Through this deep immune-cell characterization, we hope to gain insights into the immunological processes underlying postoperative complications.

interventions.name:
Changes in surface markers of neutrophils (including CD11b, CD62L, CXCR2, CD101, CD10) and monocytes (including CD14, CD16)

Time points: 0 h (before skin incision), 2 h, 4 h, 6 h, 12 h, 24 h (after skin incision)
